drawing-exam-ready-graphs: What separates a graph that earns full marks from one that looks right but scores nothing?
unit-1-scarcity: Even the richest person on Earth cannot have everything. Why not?
What four kinds of resources go into making even a simple loaf of bread?
Why does each extra unit of one thing cost a country more and more of another?
How could ten workers make thousands of pins a day when one alone could barely make twenty?
Why do countries buy from abroad things they could make perfectly well at home?
unit-1-scarcity-part-2: Why do economists insist that a price cut does not increase demand?
Why do farmers grow more when prices rise, and what makes them grow less at every price?
When a price is too high or too low, what pulls it back to where buyers and sellers agree?
When a harvest fails or buyers rush in, which way do prices move, and how far?
unit-2-circular-flow-gdp: Why must a country's total spending, total income and total output always be equal?
If a country's output is worth more money this year, has it really produced more?
Can a country's income tell you how well its people really live?
unit-2-unemployment: Why does an economy grow in bursts and slumps instead of at a steady pace?
Who counts as unemployed, and who slips through the count?
Why are some people out of work even when the economy is booming?
How can one number tell you how much prices have risen for a whole country of shoppers?
If all pay rose as fast as prices, would inflation still hurt anyone?
unit-3-aggregate-demand-ad: If every price in a country goes up at once, why would people buy less of the country's output?
What makes a whole country suddenly stop spending, even when pay has not changed?
If a government spends 1 billion, why can the country's income end up growing by much more?
Why can a jump in oil prices make a whole economy produce less and charge more at once?
Can a country buy lower unemployment by accepting a little more inflation?
What sets the most a country can produce, and can extra spending push past it?
unit-3-aggregate-demand-ad-part-2: Why can prices and unemployment rise at the same time?
What makes prices across a whole economy keep going up?
If a slump ends by itself, why do some economists say we should not wait?
Can an economy keep growing just by people spending more?
When a slump hits, can a government spend its way out of it?
Why does a government's borrowing jump in a recession even when nobody votes for it?
unit-4-financial-assets: Why will a shop swap a meal for a printed slip of paper but not for a bag of apples?
Why would anyone sell a safe government bond for less than they paid for it?
If your savings grow every year, how can you still end up able to buy less?
If money has a price, what makes that price go up or down?
When a bank lends you money, whose money are you actually borrowing?
unit-4-monetary-policy: Why can't you open an account at a central bank, and what does it do instead?
If the Fed cannot order banks to charge more, how does it push interest rates up across the country?
How can one interest rate, set by a handful of people, slow down inflation across a whole country?
Where does the money businesses borrow come from, and what decides its price?
Why can one decision by a central bank change what a currency is worth around the world?
unit-5-fiscal-monetary-policy: If a country printed twice as much money, would everything really cost twice as much?
If a country's yearly deficit keeps shrinking, how can its debt still be growing?
When a government borrows more, can it leave firms with less to invest?
If a kitchen hires twice as many cooks, why might it not make twice as many meals?
How can a government raise the most its economy can produce, and why does it take so long?
Why can the right cure for one slump be the wrong cure for the next?
unit-6-balance-payments-accounts: When a country buys more from the world than it sells, how does it pay the difference?
Nobody sets the price of a dollar or a euro, so what decides it from one day to the next?
When a country's money loses value abroad, who wins and who loses at home?
